research_items.item_name: Structured vs. Unstructured Viva Inter-Rater Reliability: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis (2023)
research_items.key_findings: Structured viva examinations demonstrate significantly higher inter-rater reliability than unstructured traditional viva: (1) Reliability coefficient 0.7-0.8 for structured viva vs. 0.3-0.4 for unstructured viva; (2) Cronbach's alpha α=0.80 for structured viva vs. α=0.50 for conventional viva; (3) Structured viva achieved inter-rater reliability r=0.78-0.91 (p<0.0001) and inter-rater agreement 86.7%; (4) Despite structured improvements, significant examiner effects persist: variation in 'hawk' (stringent) vs 'dove' (lenient) examiners documented; (5) Even structured viva cannot fully eliminate examiner bias without additional standardization; (6) Findings demonstrate unstructured viva is fundamentally unreliable for assessment, yet structured approaches still leave residual bias.
research_items.methodology: Systematic review and meta-analysis of viva assessment studies in health professions education, pooling reliability coefficients across multiple studies using different assessment contexts
research_items.sample_size: Multiple studies included in meta-analysis; structured viva studies reviewed across different medical and health professions programs globally
research_items.geographic_scope: International health professions education; studies from North America, Europe, and other regions; focus on medical, dental, and allied health professional education
research_items.publication_details: Structured viva validity, reliability, and acceptability as an assessment tool in health professions education: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education, 2023. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12909-023-04524-6. Also available at: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10369684/
research_items.study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of published viva assessment studies
research_items.replication_status: Meta-analysis synthesizes findings from multiple independent studies; reliability coefficients consistently reported across different health professions contexts; findings replicated across different institutions and countries
research_items.methodological_limitations: Studies in meta-analysis may use different definitions of 'structured' viva. Heterogeneity in assessment contexts (medical vs. dental vs. allied health) may limit generalizability. Publication bias may favor studies showing higher reliability. Some older studies may not reflect current assessment practices.
research_items.generalizability: Highly generalizable to health professions education globally; applicable to any oral assessment context where standardization is implemented; implications extend to graduate viva defenses beyond medical education; findings demonstrate structure improves but does not eliminate bias
research_items.which_debate_claim_it_supports_or_challe: Challenges assumption that human examiners provide objective assessment free from systematic bias; supports argument that even well-designed oral assessments contain substantial examiner effects; undermines claim that viva defenses are inherently more fair than detection-based methods; demonstrates that improving viva requires significant infrastructure (standardization, training, multiple examiners) yet still produces bias
research_items.policy_implications: Institutions using oral defenses/vivas must implement structured protocols, standardized questions, and detailed rubrics to minimize bias; single examiner vivas are scientifically indefensible due to low reliability; multiple examiners required but even multiple examiners show bias; examiner training is necessary but insufficient; post-standardization of scores among examiners needed; institutions should audit viva outcomes for examiner effect and demographic disparities
research_items.how_it_changes_the_analysis: Establishes that unstructured viva (reliability 0.3-0.4) has worse reliability than many AI detection tools (accuracy 67-85%); reveals that improving viva to acceptable standards requires substantial infrastructure; demonstrates that human oral assessment is not inherently superior to other assessment methods and may be worse than well-implemented alternatives; raises question of whether resource-intensive viva improvements deliver better outcomes than simpler approaches
research_items.contradictory_findings: Some older studies report even lower reliability for unstructured viva (0.2 range) while some report higher structured viva reliability (0.85+); variation across health professions in whether structured viva achieves desired reliability levels; acceptability by students (79.8%) is high despite moderate reliability, suggesting student perception differs from measured reliability
research_items.alternative_interpretations: High reliability of structured viva may reflect standardization reducing variance rather than eliminating examiner bias; examiner effects may be addressable through better training and calibration rather than fundamental limitation; variation in reported reliability may reflect differences in implementation quality rather than method limitation; hawk/dove effects may be addressable through examiner experience and feedback mechanisms
unresolved_questions: What proportion of examiner variance in viva scores reflects true difference in candidate knowledge vs. examiner bias?
How effective are different training programs at reducing hawk/dove effects and other bias sources?
Do demographic characteristics of examiners (gender, ethnicity, discipline background) influence their scoring patterns independent of candidate performance?
What is the optimal number and composition of examiners for reliable viva assessment?
Can examiner calibration meetings and standardized rubrics further reduce bias below current 0.7-0.8 reliability levels?
How do viva reliability outcomes vary across different student populations (race, ethnicity, gender, international vs. domestic)?

research_items.what_evidence_still_missing: Comparative study of viva reliability outcomes across different demographic student populations to measure disparate impact; longitudinal study tracking how examiner bias changes with experience and training; quantitative comparison of viva reliability with other assessment methods (detection tools, traditional exams, portfolios); cost-benefit analysis of achieving 0.7+ reliability viva vs. alternative assessment approaches; analysis of actual outcomes for students assessed by 'hawk' vs 'dove' examiners to measure practical impact of examiner bias
recommended_studies: Multi-institution audit of viva outcomes by examiner characteristics (gender, ethnicity, experience level, discipline) to quantify examiner effects on outcomes
Randomized study comparing structured viva outcomes for same candidates with different examiner pairs to isolate examiner variance from candidate variance

High feasibility for cost-effectiveness analysis (requires financial data compilation but doable).

research_items.item_name: Ethnic and Gender Bias in Oral Examinations and OSCEs: Medical Education (2020-2024)
research_items.key_findings: Multiple studies document demographic bias in oral assessments in medical education: (1) Gender bias: Examiner gender and lifetime experience influence scoring patterns; some examiners show bias when scoring communication skills; (2) Ethnicity/accent bias: Students with non-native English accents subject to unconscious bias during OSCEs; research shows non-native accents cause stereotyping and negative judgment; overseas-trained candidates facing difficulties related to communication style differences; (3) Magnitude: Candidates from ethnic minorities and with non-native accents rated lower than equally qualified counterparts; patients evaluate non-native accented doctors as less competent despite equal qualifications; (4) Bias mechanisms: Examiner perception of 'professional competence' influenced by accent; communication style expectations (directness, formality, answer length) vary and disadvantage international candidates; confirmation bias where initial impressions guide subsequent evaluation; (5) Variability: While some studies find no systematic bias, others find substantial effects, suggesting some examiners biased while others are not.
research_items.methodology: Multiple methodological approaches: (1) Randomized controlled pilot trial of accent bias (non-native English vs. native English, same content); (2) Analysis of real OSCE data examining gender and ethnicity patterns; (3) Qualitative analysis of oral examination fairness in UK medical qualification (MRCGP); (4) Comparative study of structured vs. unstructured exams and bias levels; (5) Implicit bias and frame of reference training intervention studies
research_items.sample_size: Varied across studies; RCT pilot studies typically n=30-100 participants; OSCE data analyses from large cohorts; MRCGP analysis examined examination pass rates across demographic groups
research_items.geographic_scope: Primarily UK (MRCGP, medical schools) and Australia (OSCE studies); North America (medical education programs); represents international student populations; findings generalizable to any institution with diverse student and examiner populations
research_items.publication_details: Multiple primary sources: (1) Ethnic and Gender Bias in Objective Structured Clinical Examinations. Education in the Health Professions, 2021. https://journals.lww.com/ehpf/fulltext/2021/04020/ethnic_and_gender_bias_in_objective_structured.2.aspx; (2) A randomised controlled pilot trial of the influence of non-native English accents on examiners' scores in OSCEs. BMC Medical Education, 2020. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12909-020-02198-y; (3) Oral examinations—equal opportunities, ethnicity, and fairness in the MRCGP. PMC, 2006. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1127149/; (4) Standardized Oral Examinations Allow for Assessment of Medical Student Clinical Knowledge and Decrease Racial Grading Differences in a Surgery Clerkship. PMC, 2024. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10570985/
research_items.study_design: Mixed methods: randomized controlled trials (pilot), observational analysis of real assessment data, qualitative analysis of examination processes, comparative effectiveness studies
research_items.replication_status: Findings on accent bias consistently replicated in independent studies; ethnic bias documented across multiple institutions and countries; gender bias findings consistent with broader literature on gender in assessment; concerns about bias validated by multiple methodological approaches
research_items.methodological_limitations: Small sample sizes in some RCT pilots; observational studies subject to confounding (candidate performance may differ between groups); qualitative analyses may reflect specific institutional contexts; cross-national variations in bias magnitude suggest context-dependency; some studies examine only one dimension of bias at a time (don't measure intersectionality)
research_items.generalizability: Highly generalizable to any English-language medical education context and international student populations; findings apply to health professions education broadly (dentistry, nursing, allied health); concerns about accent bias apply to any field assessed via oral examination; bias mechanisms likely apply to non-medical contexts (law, business, academia); concern most acute in countries with significant international student populations
research_items.which_debate_claim_it_supports_or_challe: Powerfully challenges assumption that human examiners provide unbiased assessment; documents specific, measurable bias against protected demographic groups; suggests viva defenses may perpetuate discrimination against international students, women, and ethnic minorities; demonstrates that bias is unconscious/structural, not just individual examiner prejudice; supports argument that viva may be worse than alternative assessment methods for equitable outcomes; challenges feasibility of using viva for high-stakes decisions without substantial safeguards
research_items.policy_implications: Institutions should not use unstructured vivas for any high-stakes assessment without addressing bias; if using oral assessment, must conduct demographic audits of outcomes; examiner implicit bias training required but research suggests insufficient alone; combine with rubric standardization, multiple examiners, and blinding where possible; consider alternatives to oral assessment for populations facing bias; international student support needed if viva required; legal liability concerns for institutions perpetuating biased assessment
research_items.how_it_changes_the_analysis: Reveals that viva bias specifically targets protected demographic groups (women, ethnic minorities, international students), raising equity and discrimination concerns beyond just reliability; suggests that improving viva may require corrective measures (affirmative action in scoring) that are ethically complex; demonstrates that demographic disparities in viva outcomes may not reflect candidate knowledge differences but examiner bias; questions whether viva can ever be truly fair given unconscious bias documentation
research_items.contradictory_findings: Some studies find no systematic ethnic or gender bias while others find substantial effects; magnitude of bias varies across studies and may depend on examiner characteristics; some findings suggest structured exams reduce bias, others suggest bias persists even with structure; variation in whether accent effects are consistent or variable across examiners
research_items.alternative_interpretations: Apparent bias against non-native speakers might reflect actual differences in communication quality rather than pure examiner bias (alternative hypothesis not tested in most studies); gender and ethnic differences in scoring might reflect genuine differences in candidate performance rather than bias; some examiners may be biased while others are not, suggesting bias is addressable through examiner selection and training; accent effects might be valid assessment criteria (communication is important for doctors) rather than pure bias
unresolved_questions: What is the prevalence of bias among examiners overall? Do some examiners show no detectable bias while others show substantial bias?
Can implicit bias training effectively reduce examiner bias in real oral assessments, or only awareness without behavior change?
What is the magnitude of bias impact on actual pass/fail decisions? How many borderline candidates are failed due to bias?
Do female examiners show different bias patterns than male examiners? Do examiner diversity reduce bias or introduce new forms?
What specific examiner characteristics (experience level, training, discipline, personality) predict likelihood of bias?
Can blinding (anonymous scoring) or other techniques effectively eliminate oral assessment bias?
How does accent bias interact with other forms of discrimination (gender, ethnicity, disability)?
What are the long-term career implications for students wrongly failed or unfairly scored due to examiner bias?

research_items.item_name: Examiner Training Effectiveness in Reducing Bias: Mixed Results and Limitations (2018-2024)
research_items.key_findings: Research on examiner training shows mixed effectiveness: (1) Training reduces some biases: Implicit bias training, frame of reference training, and rubric training show promise at reducing bias in controlled settings; (2) Limited effectiveness documented: Greater leniency exhibited by untrained examiners compared to trained ones, but trained examiners still show bias; (3) Training effectiveness varies: Different training approaches have different effectiveness; effects may not persist over time; benefits may not transfer to actual high-stakes assessments; (4) Insufficient alone: Training must be combined with structural measures (standardized rubrics, multiple examiners, calibration meetings) to achieve acceptable reliability; (5) Ongoing issue: Despite decades of research on examiner bias and training, bias persists in contemporary assessments (2024), suggesting training effectiveness plateaus
research_items.methodology: Multiple approaches: (1) Experimental studies comparing trained vs. untrained examiners; (2) Before/after studies measuring examiner behavior change following training; (3) Comparative studies of different training content and formats; (4) Real-world implementation studies tracking bias reduction in actual assessment settings; (5) Longitudinal studies examining whether training benefits persist
research_items.sample_size: Varied: experimental studies typically n=30-100 examiners; real-world implementations tracked outcomes across multiple examiners and hundreds of students
research_items.geographic_scope: Primarily medical and health professions education; studies from North America, Europe, Australia; findings likely generalizable to other fields using oral assessment
research_items.publication_details: Examiner seniority and experience are associated with bias when scoring communication, but not examination, skills in objective structured clinical examinations in Australia. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions, 2018. https://www.jeehp.org/journal/view.php?doi=10.3352/jeehp.2018.15.17. Also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6194481/. See also recent 2024 reviews in BMC Medical Education examining training effectiveness in reducing examiner effects.
research_items.study_design: Mixed methods: experimental comparisons, quasi-experimental before/after designs, observational studies of real assessment data, systematic review of training literature
research_items.replication_status: Findings on training benefits replicated across studies; observation that untrained examiners are more lenient consistently reported; finding that training is insufficient alone replicated across contexts
research_items.methodological_limitations: Limited ability to determine causation (selection bias: trained examiners may be more conscientious); short-term follow-up in many studies (benefits may fade); real-world measurement challenges (difficult to control for confounds in actual assessments); some studies use small sample sizes of examiners; heterogeneity in training content and duration makes synthesis difficult
research_items.generalizability: Findings generalizable to health professions education globally; concerns about training limitations likely apply to any field using oral assessment; suggests that training investments may have diminishing returns; findings apply across different examination formats (OSCE, viva, clinical exam)
research_items.which_debate_claim_it_supports_or_challe: Challenges claim that examiner training alone solves bias problems; supports argument that addressing examiner bias requires substantial infrastructure (not just training); demonstrates training benefits plateau, suggesting fundamental limits to reducing bias through training alone; undermines recommendation for universal viva expansion without addressing examiner quality; suggests poorly trained viva examiners would produce worse outcomes than well-implemented detection systems
research_items.policy_implications: Examiner training should not be considered sufficient solution to bias; must be combined with standardization, rubrics, multiple examiners; institutions expanding viva use must invest in examiner infrastructure or face worse outcomes than baseline; training program development and delivery requires substantial resources; periodic retraining needed as bias recurs; ongoing monitoring and audit of examiner performance required; institutions should measure effectiveness of their training interventions, not assume benefit
research_items.how_it_changes_the_analysis: Shifts from 'should we use viva' to 'can we resource adequate examiner training and support'; reveals that recommending vivas without addressing examiner quality would likely produce worse outcomes than current systems; demonstrates that infrastructure for reliable vivas is more complex and resource-intensive than commonly recognized; raises question of whether institutions should expand viva when they cannot adequately train examiners; suggests that research promoting vivas as solution should include cost of necessary examiner training and infrastructure
research_items.contradictory_findings: Some studies show substantial training benefits while others show minimal benefits; variation in whether training benefits persist over time; differences in whether training reduces bias uniformly or only for some examiners; inconsistent findings on which training approaches are most effective
research_items.alternative_interpretations: Training benefits may be understated due to measurement challenges in real-world settings; selection effects (more conscientious examiners seek training) may inflate observed benefits; training content differences may account for variable effectiveness; longer follow-up may be needed to assess durable behavior change; training + structural supports may be more effective than training alone (interaction effects not always measured)
unresolved_questions: What is the optimal content, duration, and format for examiner training to maximize bias reduction?
Do training benefits persist over years, or do they diminish over time requiring periodic retraining?
Which examiners benefit most from training? Are some examiners resistant to bias reduction training?
Can examiner training reduce bias enough to achieve acceptable reliability (0.7+) or is there a ceiling?
What is the cost-benefit ratio of examiner training vs. other bias mitigation approaches (standardization, technology, alternative assessment methods)?
Do different types of bias (gender, ethnicity, accent, halo effect) respond differently to training?
What happens in resource-constrained settings where comprehensive examiner training is not feasible?

research_items.item_name: Halo Effect and Hawk/Dove Effects in Viva Assessment: Persistent Bias Mechanisms (2020-2024)
research_items.key_findings: Cognitive biases persist in oral assessment despite standardization efforts: (1) Halo effect: Examiners' overall first impressions of candidates lead to failure to discriminate between discrete aspects of performance; if first impression is positive, all subsequent scores tend to be high; conversely, negative first impression suppresses scores on objective components; (2) Hawk/dove effects: Consistent examiner stringency variation exists where some examiners consistently mark candidates strictly (hawks) while others are consistently lenient (doves); (3) Persistence despite structure: Both halo and hawk/dove effects documented even in structured viva assessments with standardized questions and rubrics; (4) Interaction effects: Halo effects may be larger for some examiners and smaller for others; effects may depend on candidate presentation style; (5) Measurement challenge: These biases are subtle, consistent, and difficult to address because examiners may be unaware of them; unlike random error, these biases systematically advantage or disadvantage specific candidates
research_items.methodology: Multiple approaches: (1) Analysis of real viva score data examining correlations between items to detect halo effects; (2) Experimental designs comparing same candidates scored by multiple examiners to isolate examiner effects; (3) Comparative analysis of within-examiner consistency (do they have stable hawk/dove patterns); (4) Qualitative analysis of examiner decision-making processes; (5) Meta-analysis synthesizing findings across studies documenting these effects
research_items.sample_size: Varies: observational studies of real vivas n=100-500 candidates × multiple examiners; experimental studies typically n=30-50 examiners; meta-analyses including 20+ studies
research_items.geographic_scope: Primarily medical and health professions education internationally; studies from UK, Australia, North America, Europe; findings likely generalizable to any field using oral assessment
research_items.publication_details: Structured viva validity, reliability, and acceptability as an assessment tool in health professions education: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education, 2023. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12909-023-04524-6. See also: The sights and insights of examiners in objective structured clinical examinations. PMC, 2018. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5801428/. And: An Analysis of the Generalizability and Stability of the Halo Effect During the COVID-19 Pandemic Outbreak. Frontiers in Psychology, 2021. https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.631871/full
research_items.study_design: Mixed methods: observational analysis of real assessment data, experimental designs, systematic reviews, qualitative examiner interview studies
research_items.replication_status: Halo effects consistently documented across multiple studies and contexts; hawk/dove effects persistently replicated; effects documented in both medical education and other domains; COVID-era study confirmed effects persist even in remote/online assessments
research_items.methodological_limitations: Difficulty isolating halo from genuine performance consistency (if candidate is strong on one dimension, they may be strong on others); examiner assignment to candidates may be non-random (stronger examiners may assess stronger candidates, confounding analysis); correlation-based evidence of halo effects can be ambiguous; experimental studies examining halo effects may not reflect real-world stakes or pressures; some studies cannot measure degree of halo effect separately from hawk/dove effects
research_items.generalizability: Highly generalizable to all oral assessment contexts; documented across different examination types (OSCE, viva, clinical exam); effects persist regardless of assessment structure or standardization; findings apply internationally; likely apply to any human judgment assessment (not unique to academia)
research_items.which_debate_claim_it_supports_or_challe: Challenges claim that structured assessment eliminates bias; documents persistent cognitive biases that resist standardization efforts; demonstrates that viva assessment is subject to systematic biases (halo, hawk/dove) similar to detection tool biases; suggests that human judgment bias may be as problematic as algorithmic bias; undermines argument that human viva is inherently superior to other assessment methods
research_items.policy_implications: Institutions using vivas must acknowledge these biases cannot be eliminated through rubrics or structure alone; multiple examiners required to reduce variance from individual hawk/dove patterns; post-standardization of scores may be necessary (adjusting for known examiner effects); blind assessment (hiding candidate identity/prior performance) may reduce halo effect but may be infeasible for oral exams; video recording and second-rater review may help; institutions should audit viva score patterns for halo and hawk/dove effects
research_items.how_it_changes_the_analysis: Reveals that viva assessment contains cognitive biases (halo, hawk/dove) that are persistent, subtle, and resistant to typical mitigation attempts; suggests that the gap between measured viva reliability and ideal reliability is due to these persistent biases rather than measurement error; demonstrates that even well-implemented vivas will retain substantial examiner effects; raises question of whether investing in viva improvement is efficient use of resources given persistence of these biases
research_items.contradictory_findings: Some examiners show strong halo effects while others show minimal effects; magnitude of hawk/dove variation differs across contexts; some findings suggest halo effects may be addressable through certain training approaches, others suggest effects are highly resistant to intervention; conflicting evidence on whether halo effects are stable over time vs. context-dependent
research_items.alternative_interpretations: Observed score correlations may reflect genuine candidate consistency (candidate strong across domains) rather than halo effect (examiner inflating correlated scores); hawk/dove effects may reflect valid differences in examiner standards/expectations rather than biases; examiners may have legitimate reasons for their consistent patterns; first impression effects may be partly valid (first responses are often revealing of knowledge)
unresolved_questions: What is the magnitude of halo and hawk/dove effects in terms of score points? How many candidates are affected by misclassification due to these biases?
Are certain examiner characteristics associated with stronger halo effects? Can examiners be trained to reduce halo effects?
Do hawk/dove effects reflect stable examiner characteristics or do they change over time and across contexts?
How do halo and hawk/dove effects interact with other forms of bias (gender, ethnicity, accent)?
Can blinded assessment or other techniques effectively eliminate halo effects in oral assessment?
What is the impact of halo and hawk/dove effects on candidate outcomes? How many borderline candidates pass/fail based on these biases?

Counterfactual analysis of viva outcomes: retrospectively adjust scores for estimated examiner effects and determine how many pass/fail decisions would change
Mechanism study analyzing video recordings of vivas to identify specific behaviors (questioning, follow-up, interpretation) that differ by examiner type (hawk vs. dove, high vs. low halo)
Longitudinal study tracking examiner patterns over 3-5 years to measure stability of hawk/dove and halo effects and impact of experience/training
research_items.feasibility_of_filling_gap: High feasibility for meta-analysis (literature synthesis, moderate cost). High feasibility for observational study of examiner patterns (requires institutional viva data, privacy manageable). Medium-high feasibility for intervention study (can be conducted at multiple institutions, moderate cost, important outcomes). Medium feasibility for counterfactual analysis (requires detailed score data, statistical modeling). Medium feasibility for mechanism study (video analysis labor-intensive but doable). Medium-high feasibility for longitudinal study (requires sustained data collection but institutional partnerships manageable).
